extracted.intended_audience: classical philologists, students and scholars of Aristotle, editors and translators of ancient Greek texts
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly commentary and hermeneutic guidance for reading, emending, translating, and explaining passages in Aristotle's Poetics (and related Aristotelian corpus), with attention to Greek grammar, accentuation, medical/technical terminology, and textual transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference to the Aristotelian corpus
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that the Poetics refers to other works (Organon, Physics, Metaphysics, Problems, Politics) and that grasping Aristotle's remarks often requires familiarizing oneself with substantial parts of his system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting a passage in the Poetics consult related Aristotelian texts (Organon, Physics, Metaphysics, Problems, Politics) to resolve technical terms and concepts; do not treat isolated passages as self-sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for technical/medical sense (katharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret technical words (e.g. katharsis) in their contemporaneous technical/medical and physiological senses rather than modern or popular metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Aristotle's medical theory (Problems, Hippocratic references, doctrine of humours) to read katharsis as 'adjustment' or medical 'clearing' rather than merely 'emotional discharge' or 'relief'; avoid transplanting later or modern senses without reconciling them with the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philological evidence and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Base interpretations on philological evidence — scholiasts, Theophrastus, Herodian, lexica, and other extant authorities — and check whether commentators misquote or garble authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer readings supported by contemporary or near-contemporary sources; flag and correct misquotations (e.g., garblings of Theophrastus) and weigh scholiastic testimony critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to original usage and avoidance of wrong senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute to Aristotle senses he did not intend; the esoteric style is not 'using words in wrong senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing modern or speculative meanings onto words; if a commentator's reading requires reading Aristotle as having used a word in a 'wrong' sense, re-evaluate the reading or its emendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accentuation and intonation must be understood technically
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations involving Greek accents (acute, grave, perispomenon, oxytone, unaccented) require familiarity with ancient accentuation theory (dynamis vs energeia) and rules (e.g., Herodian's notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an interpretation hinges on accent/intonation (e.g., ov negative vs ov where), consult grammatical authorities and the system of dynamis/energeia; treat written accent marks as conventional signs of intonation and apply the broader Aristotelian phonological doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emendations must preserve authorial formulae and internal coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectural emendations (e.g., Bernays's supplement) must fit Aristotelian formulae and not destroy the grammatical or conceptual structure of the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject emendations that force unnatural constructions, contradict other explicit statements (e.g., on metre or formulaic usage), or render the sentence ungrammatical or incoherent; prefer emendations supported by the author's typical usage and by parallel formulae in the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use etymology carefully (historical vs folk etymology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical etymology is valuable and scientific, but speculative etymological history or folk etymology (deriving misplaced senses from later associations) is unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base large interpretive claims on fanciful etymologies; test etymological proposals against usage evidence, dictionaries, and historic attestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for meter/genre-specific usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Words describing poetic kinds (e.g., epopoiia, 'hexametric fabrication') may have technical metrical or genre-specific meanings; ordinary usage and technical usage can diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting terms about genre or metre, check how Aristotle and other authors use them (e.g., epopoiia applied to prose fiction or mixed metres) and avoid assuming modern genre boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect Greek grammatical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek syntax and morphological rules (e.g., inability to annex definite to indefinite, meaning of cases and accents) constrain possible translations and reconstructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render and emend in ways that preserve Greek grammar; do not produce translations that would be un-Greek (e.g., incorrect attachment of definites) or that ignore grammatical forms (cases, agreement, enclitics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual synthesis across scattered passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruct a term's meaning (e.g., tragic/Tragedy, katharsis) by synthesizing scattered references across the corpus rather than relying on single isolated sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and compare occurrences in Politics, Problems, Poetics, Parva Naturalia, etc., to form an interpretation consistent with the author's systemic usage; prefer interpretations grounded in multiple attestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of later corruptions or deliberate alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the possibility of later interpolations, redactions, or deliberate Christian alterations that may have modified the text or its transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate readings and variant manuscripts in light of textual history; where a passage seems anomalous (e.g., abrupt shifts, theological discomfort), assess whether transmissional changes could explain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate genre labels with their etymologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid simplistic inferences that equate a name's literal etymology (e.g., 'goat-song') with the origin or essential character of the genre without corroborating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical and contextual evidence (scholia, inscriptions, prizes, comparative customs) to test etymological origin theories rather than treating literal name-meanings as decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer traditional accentuation system either wholly or not at all
rubrics_metrics.description: Accent marks and accentual doctrine are a coherent system; partial adoption (mixing doctrines) leads to inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either adopt the full traditional accentuation framework (including notions of dynamis/energeia and rules about enclitics) when explaining accent-related phenomena, or avoid relying on accent-based explanations that presuppose inconsistent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain ambiguity of formulaic constructions (etymological/metaphorical mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Aristotle uses species terms for a nameless genus (e.g., hexameter used for 'fiction'), explain whether usage arises from confusion, metaphor, or conscious lexical extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether a species-for-genus usage is accidental (confusion) or deliberate (metaphor/lexical necessity) and support the conclusion with examples and parallel usages in the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cautious tone and scholarly rigor in proposing theses
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overconfident or uncourteous assertions when defending novel readings; scholarly claims should be carefully considered and supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing interpretations or emendations, present philological support and acknowledge uncertainties; severe language about opponents' errors is unwarranted without robust demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/logical readings must respect authorial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When Aristotle appeals to numerical or logical demonstrations (e.g., Homeric sums), prefer readings that accord with his demonstrated practice elsewhere rather than projecting modern conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check other Aristotelian writings for consistent treatment of divisions, numeration (hours, parts), and logical constructs before endorsing a mathematical reading that would be out of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret musical/performative terms with physiological and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms about song, pitch, and 'tragic' voice should be read with attention to ancient musical physiology (voice-change, pitch irregularity) and cultural function (how pitch conveys sorrow/terror).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporary physiological descriptions (e.g., adolescence voice change) and passages in Problems/Natural History to ground claims about 'tragic song' as irregular pitch symbolic of grief; avoid purely literary or modern musical analogies without corpus support.
